english_title: Gustavo Montaña Montaña — first voluntary-statement session, 3 December 2018
purpose: To examine Montaña’s operational and intelligence work in the Casanare GAULA, reconstruct particular killings and the handling of reserved funds, and begin testing his account of orders, fabricated combat reports and responsibilities within the military chain of command.
named_people_roles: Montaña appears as a former GAULA noncommissioned officer, represented by Jorge Enrique Lizarazo Oviedo. Magistrate Catalina Díaz Gómez and auxiliary magistrate Juan Carlos Losada participate, alongside further judicial questioning and the Public Ministry. Montaña identifies Major Gustavo Soto Bracamonte as his commander and Colonel Torres Escalante as brigade commander. Lieutenant Toro, Corporal Gélver Pérez García and soldiers Pedro José Velandia Rolón, González Almario and Ávila Celis appear in specific operational accounts. He names Alberto Pinzón Pardo in the handling of money and discusses DAS investigators’ participation in the Las Tapias operation.
main_accounts_claims: Montaña alleges that command radio briefings rewarded deaths and disparaged units without results, and that Soto told him captures were insufficient. At Palo Bajito, he describes intercepting two men brought by a soldier, receiving Soto’s instruction to kill them, and soldiers placing and firing weapons beside the bodies. He admits signing a false combat account. In a subsequent operation associated with Ferney Achagua Reyes and Darío Ruiz, he describes detention after a proposed ammunition purchase, an order to kill, shootings by Pérez and Velandia, and Toro reporting two deaths to Torres by telephone. Another account follows the capture of Abelardo Reyes and a second man, unsuccessful searches for supposedly hidden rifles, repeated calls from Soto and their eventual killing at Matepalma. He describes coordinating the cover story before investigators arrived. He also discusses signing checks while Soto and Pinzón handled withdrawals. For Las Tapias, he describes an apparent attack on a vehicle during an extortion operation, disputed participation by commanders and investigators, and questionable informant-payment paperwork. He denies seeing the missing money attributed to the victims and distinguishes firsthand observations from later case-file information.
stated_positions_responses: Montaña admits following unlawful killing orders but says he had believed the victims were offenders and now feels deceived by superiors who said otherwise. He does not equate that claimed belief with actual combat: he acknowledges that victims did not fight. The questioners press him on his experience, command knowledge, intelligence, weapons and payments; counsel promises to replace an earlier submission whose CD was blank.
outcome_open_questions: The hearing is suspended at 18:00, with continuation provisionally discussed for 20 February. The JEP emphasizes corroboration, possible contradictions with other witnesses, victims’ observations and further consideration of reparation. Remaining incidents, the funds trail, specific superior orders and the basis of security concerns require additional evidence.

english_title: Edwin Leonardo Toro Ramírez — killings in Antioquia, Delta operations and the Casanare GAULA method
purpose: Toro’s first session traces his service from the Jorge Eduardo Sánchez Battalion in Antioquia to Delta units and GAULA Casanare. It examines specific killings, operational pressure, alleged cooperation with paramilitary guides, falsified combat accounts and how practices carried between assignments.
named_people_roles: Edwin Leonardo Toro Ramírez speaks as the former lieutenant involved in the operations. Catalina Díaz Gómez and Óscar Parra Vera question him; Luis Hernando Castellanos Fonseca is his defense lawyer, and Mónica Sánchez Medina represents the Public Ministry. He names Corporals Daza and Cuestas in Antioquia incidents, Sergeant Amaya in Casanare, Emilio Enrique Torres Ariza as brigade chief of staff, William Torres Escalante as brigade commander and Wilson de Jesús Soto Bracamonte as GAULA commander. The guide called “Mimisica” appears in his description of GAULA recruitment.
main_accounts_claims: Toro describes pressure for deaths and leave incentives in Antioquia, including radio interventions he attributes to Mario Montoya. He alleges that armed paramilitary guides accompanied an Ituango operation. He admits ordering Luz Stelly Morales’s killing and misleading her family, and personally shooting two detained men near Buenos Aires. He also describes knowingly reporting the deaths of “Chepe Posada” and “Pecho de Lata” as combat and ordering two men killed after his group posed as guerrillas. In Casanare, he admits shooting a wounded, unarmed man found after the Labranza Grande operation, and killing Jair Tarache Cruz after detention. He says he reported a death before Tarache was actually killed, received material to place with the body, and later replaced operational-file pages bearing identifying photographs. For GAULA, he describes people supplied through “Mimisica,” weapons and surgical gloves supplied by Soto, and staging bodies and gunshot-residue evidence. He qualifies the command allegation: Soto did not necessarily issue an explicit verbal killing order; Toro understood the supplied kit and expected result as the instruction. He also distinguishes what he communicated to Torres Ariza from what he actually told Torres Escalante.
stated_positions_responses: Toro acknowledges his own decisions and says he never refused the GAULA practice. He links his behavior to an acquired emphasis on producing deaths but does not treat that explanation as denying his actions. The magistrates press him to distinguish direct orders, inferred knowledge and firsthand observation. He expresses remorse and requests suspension after a prolonged session.
outcome_open_questions: The court suspends the hearing at 18:17 and plans a continuation. Toro is asked to reconstruct dates and revisit unanswered identification questions. Responsibility of superiors and details of particular operations require further contrastation; his accounts are not treated here as findings against the people he names.

english_title: Helbert Pérez García — voluntary statement, 26 March 2019
purpose: To obtain Pérez’s account of his military service, the Casanare GAULA’s organization and specific deaths reported as combat, including his own actions, alleged orders, prior silence and possible contributions to victims’ truth and reparation.
named_people_roles: Pérez speaks as a former corporal in operational units, represented by Jimmy Fernando Niño Torres. Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera presides with Juan Carlos Losada Perdomo and Public Ministry participation. Major Gustavo Soto Bracamonte is identified as GAULA commander; Sergeant Gustavo Montaña and Lieutenant Edwin Toro figure in the first killing account. Soldier Pedro José Velandia is identified as a shooter. Corporals Pereira and Tegue appear in accounts of resistance to orders, Lieutenant Suancha in later operations, and Ávila Celis and Celis Bedoya in alleged handling of weapons placed with bodies.
main_accounts_claims: Pérez traces his service through Boyacá, counterguerrilla units and BIRNO before attachment to the Casanare GAULA. In this session he initially identifies the GAULA as where he first encountered unlawful killings. For the El Venado/Punto Nuevo incident discussed as the deaths of Yuri Ferney Achagua and Darío Ruiz, he says Montaña told him the captives had to be killed. He admits firing toward one man but claims he deliberately missed, left, and returned after Velandia had killed both. He describes an organizational sequence from intelligence reports to operational orders approved by Soto and a ‘kit’ of weapons and ammunition used to support fabricated combat claims. He says he released intended victims from the Villanueva palm-growing area and later helped a man survive an operation involving Suancha by pretending to shoot him. He alleges reprimands and threats after such resistance. He also recounts the Villavicencio capture and transport of the man called ‘La Barbie’ and says Soto instructed detainees to remain silent while providing a lawyer. Other incidents involve his alleged delivery of ammunition rather than shooting and his assistance with body recovery at Hato El Burro.
stated_positions_responses: Pérez acknowledges participation, false combat accounts and silence, but disputes being the killer or even present in some cases attributed to him. He says commanders presented victims as serious offenders and that fear constrained resistance. Judicial questions challenge obedience, verification and his treatment of alleged offenders. He expresses remorse, willingness to disclose fuller truth and a wish to ask victims’ forgiveness.
outcome_open_questions: The hearing is suspended at 18:33, with additional factual matters and restorative possibilities left for continuation. Some dates, the extent of his role and responsibility for particular shots remain disputed. Security concerns are to be addressed separately after closing the testimony destined for victims; no protective-measures ruling appears in this record.

english_title: Faiber Alberto Amaya Ruiz — six incidents across Delta 4, GAULA and brigade intelligence
purpose: Amaya presents a chronological account of six proceedings spanning Delta 4, temporary GAULA service and the Brigade 16 intelligence section. The session examines personal shootings, assistance in staging deaths, operational paperwork and reward payments, including an incident he says had remained in military justice.
named_people_roles: Faiber Alberto Amaya Ruiz describes serving as a sergeant and Delta 4 commander, then as an operations assistant in GAULA and in brigade intelligence. Diego Andrés Vargas Acuña represents him. Judicial questioners include Juan Carlos Losada Perdomo, Hugo Escobar Fernández de Castro and Óscar Parra Vera. Edwin Toro, Soto Bracamonte, Carlos Alberto Oliveros Arrieta and Lieutenant Casallas feature in his operational accounts; Jaime Alberto Rivera appears in GAULA documentation. He also identifies brigade commanders and staff when describing instructions and reports, while qualifying conversations he did not hear.
main_accounts_claims: In Jair Tarache’s case, Amaya says the planned target was Tarache’s father, but Toro later detained and shot the son. Amaya admits firing a weapon using the dead man’s finger to create residue and helping transport the body, despite saying he had objected to the killing. For San Luis de Aricaporo, he admits shooting the detained man called Guido Mafla and ordering two other detained people killed, although they had no weapons. He says he informed brigade operations staff of that fact. In Río Chiquito, he recounts Toro bringing two men from Villavicencio, soldiers shooting them, weapons being planted and Amaya preparing the operational order afterward. He describes a similar retrospective order after Giovanni Peñata Hernández’s killing. For Arnulfo Tumaipán, he identifies his reward-payment signature and alleges that named recipients received only small portions while Soto retained money for intermediaries and weapons. At Las Tapias, he says he delivered a bag on Oliveros’s instructions, accompanied detained youths with Casallas, and witnessed the staged aftermath; he alleges DAS personnel arranged the scene. He describes this participation without claiming to have fired there.
stated_positions_responses: Amaya accepts that knowing participation and concealment made him responsible even where he did not shoot. He recalls assurances from Toro and Soto that nothing would happen because military justice would investigate. He calls the harm irreversible, expresses remorse and says victims should help determine appropriate restorative work rather than his choosing a symbolic gesture for them.
outcome_open_questions: The court requests documents concerning the incident remaining in military justice and invites written additions to unresolved details. Victims’ later questions will be transmitted for response. Amaya commits to further truth-telling and responsibility; the session ends at 17:32 on 29 April 2019.

english_title: Alexander González Almario — GAULA operations, captured civilians and disputed combat accounts, 30 April 2019
purpose: The JEP questions former GAULA Casanare soldier Alexander González Almario about multiple operations, including previously unlisted events, his own participation and the difference between genuine combat and killings of detained people. The hearing also examines command responsibility, later versions given to investigators and proposed reparation.
named_people_roles: Alexander González Almario is the principal account-giver; Jorge Enrique Lizarazo Oviedo represents him. Juan Carlos Losada Perdomo and Hugo Escobar Fernández de Castro conduct questioning, with prosecutor Andrea Natalí Bermúdez Sánchez. Major Gustavo Enrique Soto Bracamonte commanded GAULA; Jesús Eduardo Corzo Pita, Helbert Pérez and Lieutenant Puentes feature in operational accounts. Material victims include Pablo Emilio Vázquez Pérez and the three men discussed in the Alto Cupiagua episode. Some other victims remain unidentified or disputed in the hearing.
main_accounts_claims: González describes approaching a suspected recruiter in Trinidad, transporting him to El Tablón and a subsequent death followed by placement of a rifle; the magistrates identify this as an event not on their list and ask for search-related assistance. At Curipao, he recounts following two bus passengers with another soldier and a DAS detective, detaining them and handing them to Soto. He distinguishes the earlier reported combat involving “Arbolito,” which he did not witness, from the subsequent killing of the detained passengers. He describes taking Pablo Emilio Vázquez from a Yopal house to Quebrada Seca under Corzo’s command and acknowledges that he was convicted over that case. For Alto Cupiagua, he says four people were detained, Pérez ordered their deaths, and he took one man away and allowed him to escape. He alleges weapons were later placed on bodies and lawyers helped coordinate inaccurate accounts. He denies receiving reward money that Soto allegedly asked him to say he had distributed. In contrast, he defends several other operations as genuine combat or responses to extortion, including La Mesa and the April 2007 encounter discussed after lunch.
stated_positions_responses: González acknowledges unlawful actions and following orders but locates the change in practices under Soto. The magistrates challenge the idea that established personnel suddenly began acting unlawfully only after that commander arrived. He expresses remorse and willingness to seek forgiveness and perform feasible social work, while retaining his position that other questioned operations were lawful.
outcome_open_questions: The hearing ends at 17:23 with requests for a fuller written account, clearer separation of lawful and unlawful operations, additional command-chain information and concrete reparative proposals. Victim identities, dates in some recollections, earlier practices and conflicting versions still require comparison with files and other witnesses.

english_title: Fabio Eugenio Sajona Camaño — recruitment, false combat reports and disputed participation in GAULA killings
purpose: Sajona’s first session examines his GAULA Casanare duties, the development of unlawful-killing practices and his participation in multiple incidents. It separates his admissions from disputed testimony by other soldiers and asks for fuller identification of proceedings still held in military justice.
named_people_roles: Fabio Eugenio Sajona Camaño is the former GAULA noncommissioned officer giving the account. Óscar Parra Vera and Juan Carlos Losada Perdomo question him; Mónica Sánchez Medina intervenes for the Public Ministry, and Miltón Marino Mejía Alcalá represents him. He names Soto Bracamonte as commander, Edwin Toro and Jaime Alberto Rivera as operational officers, and “Mimisica” as an intermediary. Soldiers Guerrero Galvis, Correa Malatesta and Barragán feature in particular accounts. He identifies Gutiérrez as a colleague who could corroborate an occasion when he says he prevented further killings.
main_accounts_claims: Sajona describes an early operation in which Soto sent him with experienced soldiers to learn their method: a motorcyclist was detained, transported and killed. He says patrol reports and ammunition expenditure were manipulated to represent executions as exchanges of fire. In a Villavicencio operation, he acknowledges posing as a demobilized paramilitary selling ammunition and weapons, establishing trust with two men before Toro took control of their detention and subsequent operation. He recounts taking another man from Pore during local festivities and handing him into an operation involving Rivera and Toro. For Las Horticeras, he accepts being present with one victim but disputes allegations that he fired, identifying Correa Malatesta and Barragán as the shooters he saw and distinguishing the other two victims’ location. In Fredy Mosquera’s case, he says the mission was intended to kill from the outset, although the final shooting followed the detainee’s attempt to run; he denies torture. He also recounts a later occasion when he stopped the same procedure, returned two intended victims to Villanueva by bus and accepted responsibility for refusing the mission.
stated_positions_responses: Sajona acknowledges harm through participation and failure to intervene, while contesting statements he regards as falsely shifting blame onto him. He asks forgiveness and says he acted as someone who equated obedience with being a good soldier. The court presses for specificity rather than speculative attribution, especially about who fired, arranged documents or supplied information.
outcome_open_questions: The court requests a detailed written submission around 1 July, including supporting material and identification of military-justice cases. Additional victims’ questions and evidentiary comparison will follow. Defense counsel requests the recording and clarification of representation; the court explains the procedure and recognizes the ongoing nature of the truth contribution.

english_title: Miguel Fernando Ramírez, 13 June 2019: informant recruitment, successive victims and disputed reward records
purpose: The hearing investigates Ramírez’s contribution as an informant to GAULA Casanare killings, how victims were contacted and delivered, and the relationship between his information and official reward documentation. It also explores information he had withheld in ordinary proceedings and his present willingness to disclose it.
named_people_roles: Miguel Fernando Ramírez describes being a former BCG 29 professional soldier and combat medic, later a civilian informant. Óscar Parra Vera presides with Juan Carlos Lozada Perdomo; Álvaro Frías Cruz provides public defense and Rafael Nevardo Sánchez Gómez represents the Procuraduría. Ramírez identifies Major Soto Bracamonte, soldier González Almario and soldier Velandia Rolón as his principal GAULA contacts. He describes Camilo, known as El Paisa, as connected to the DAS. Several incidents concern members of the Achagua family; some other victims remain incompletely identified in his account.
main_accounts_claims: Ramírez says he supplied five pieces of information that led to killings and that GAULA personnel subsequently pressed him for further results. He describes earlier nursing work with paramilitary members for roughly four to six months, but denies personally observing military–paramilitary coordination during that period. He recounts meeting demobilized men socially and facilitating a supposed ammunition sale involving Yuri Ferney Achagua and another man, followed by their seizure by GAULA personnel. When José Germán Achagua sought information about his relative, Ramírez says he informed González Almario, helped arrange a motorcycle and accompanied an interception of Achagua and a second relative. Other accounts concern a proposed pistol transaction and a man he took toward Morichal under a pretext. He distinguishes seeing capture or delivery from witnessing subsequent killing. He acknowledges signing reward records and taking money, but says two records attribute information he did not provide, including one connected to César Augusto Concha Nieves. He alleges substitutions between informants’ reward forms; some identifications of other personnel came later from case materials rather than direct acquaintance.
stated_positions_responses: He expresses remorse and says fear for his safety helped explain his earlier silence and misleading accounts. He accepts that his information contributed to deaths while contesting responsibility for incidents linked to him only through reward paperwork. He declines to supply names or details he does not know and recognizes that truth or an apology cannot replace the victims’ relatives.
outcome_open_questions: The session ends at 15:26 on 13 June 2019, despite a July date in the public upload title. The magistrate describes this as an initial stage of comparing accounts and evidence. Victim identities in the later episodes, reward accounting and the roles of additional participants remain open; no reparative measure is approved.

english_title: Edwin Leonardo Toro Ramírez — GAULA recruitment, staged operations and clarification of individual killings
purpose: The continuation clarifies Toro’s roles in Delta groups and GAULA Casanare, then examines the preparation, execution and concealment of particular operations. It also asks how soldiers responded to participation, what incentives existed, and what Toro considers his contribution to victims’ reparation.
named_people_roles: Edwin Leonardo Toro Ramírez is questioned by auxiliary magistrate Fabián Camilo Martínez Guerrero, with defense lawyer Castellanos Fonseca and Public Ministry representative Andrés Armando Ramírez Gómez present. Toro identifies Soto as GAULA commander, Fabio Puentes as temporarily in charge during an operation, and Jaime Alberto Rivera as an officer who later reported deaths Toro had produced. He names Corporal Sajona in the Villavicencio arms-sale deception, Pérez García in the shooting of a detained soldier, and “Mimisica” as the intermediary who located people.
main_accounts_claims: Toro describes Delta groups as operationally controlled by brigade command and staff despite administrative membership in battalions. He adds an account of ordering a detained man moved to a place accessible for helicopter extraction before killing him. Describing GAULA practice, he says Soto demanded results, directed him to “Mimisica,” and supplied material while Toro selected a recurring group of soldiers. In Brisas del Llano, he describes pretending to sell ammunition and weapons, taking two men from the Villavicencio area into Casanare and killing them. He says Rivera later assumed reporting responsibility for another pair of bodies because Toro’s repeated results risked attracting scrutiny. During case questioning Toro acknowledges mixing incidents. In a separate account involving an extortion complaint, he describes detaining a cyclist, learning that he was a regular soldier, deciding with Pérez García to kill him, and forcibly pulling him from the vehicle before Pérez fired. Toro also describes a joint operation involving DAS personnel and clothing and a vehicle obtained from the company being extorted. He discusses competitive death totals, favorable personnel evaluations and transfer incentives as the operational environment.
stated_positions_responses: Toro accepts personal responsibility and denies that he forced soldiers to participate through threats against them or their families. He nevertheless acknowledges telling soldiers what version to give investigators. He says truthful disclosure is his principal proposed contribution to repair. Some claims about higher-level knowledge are inferential; the account distinguishes those from his direct admissions and reported conversations.
outcome_open_questions: The defense undertakes further work on dates and memory gaps and requests communications to relevant authorities; the presiding official refers that request to the Recognition Chamber. Additional questioning remains possible. The session closes at 17:25 on 27 June 2019, without a determination of responsibility for other named people.

english_title: Marco Fabián García Céspedes, 5 July 2019: preparation time granted before substantive voluntary testimony
purpose: The JEP installs García Céspedes’s voluntary statement but considers a defence request for additional preparation time. The session explains the required scope of truth contribution and the conditions attached to existing benefits, rather than examining the underlying killings.
named_people_roles: Óscar Parra Vera presides as a magistrate of the Sala de Reconocimiento. Marco Fabián García Céspedes attends as the compareciente and confirms that he understands the stated obligations. Luis Eduardo Lozano Rodríguez acts as defence counsel; he says he represented García in some ordinary criminal proceedings years earlier but was formally recognized for this JEP appearance only the previous day. Germán Rincón Cuéllar represents the Procuraduría and addresses the postponement request. Victims’ lawyer Fernando Rodríguez Quecan is mentioned in the arrangements for later participation.
main_accounts_claims: Counsel requests postponement because he has not yet discussed the new disclosures García proposes to make or prepared an exhaustive account suited to the JEP process. His earlier involvement in ordinary criminal cases, ending around 2012–2013, did not cover every matter that might arise. The Procuraduría supports allowing preparation, noting that the defence strategy in ordinary proceedings may differ from the approach required for a voluntary, detailed contribution to truth. Parra grants the request but emphasizes that the next account must extend beyond matters already investigated or adjudicated. He asks for organized information about incidents, military units, actual command practices, dates, case files and participants, including events unknown to ordinary or military justice. He also directs García to reflect on harm to victims and possible restorative contributions. No operational incident is narrated or tested during this session.
stated_positions_responses: García acknowledges understanding the obligations. Counsel frames postponement as necessary to protect effective defence and prepare new disclosures; the Procuraduría raises no objection. Parra balances that request with a clear warning that benefits depend on compliance and that complete truth cannot be reduced to repeating prior criminal case records.
outcome_open_questions: At 10:03 the hearing is suspended until 26 July 2019 at 13:30. The future session is to begin with judicial questioning and later include victims’ representation. The content of García’s proposed disclosures and any restorative commitments remain open.

english_title: Germán Gutiérrez Mariño — voluntary statement, 25 July 2019
purpose: To reconstruct Gutiérrez Mariño’s service in the Casanare GAULA and his knowledge of several deaths reported as combat results, distinguishing his own participation, observations, prior criminal proceedings and proposed contribution to truth and reparation.
named_people_roles: Gutiérrez Mariño speaks as a former professional soldier questioned by the JEP, the Public Ministry and victims’ representatives. He identifies Major Gustavo Soto as GAULA commander; Sergeant Gustavo Montaña, Captain Rivera, Lieutenant Toro and Corporal Julio César Tegue Medina as commanders in particular deployments. Soldiers Ángel Ortega, Caballero, Humberto Malpica, Cardona, Ávila Celis and Ospina appear in his accounts of capture, transport, shooting or security duties. He also discusses Corporal Gélver Pérez and Captain Solano. These are roles he attributes to people in this statement, not findings of their responsibility.
main_accounts_claims: Gutiérrez describes arriving at the GAULA in late 2006 and encountering killings concealed as operational results. In the first incident, provisionally associated by the questioner with Andrés Rodríguez Ruiz, he says a detained man was transported away from an alleged extortion operation and shot while Gutiérrez blocked the road. He says Montaña subsequently organized the soldiers’ account for military justice. For Matepantano on 11 January 2007, he alleges that Toro ordered two detained men killed; he describes refusing, being threatened, and seeing Ángel Ortega and Caballero shoot. He admits later firing into the air under orders. His Villanueva/Refocosta account similarly describes men brought to the unit, shooting and simulated fire, followed by transport of bodies. He alleges that soldiers later retaliated against him for telling prosecutors what happened, while disputing responsibility for a conviction. Other passages address an April killing involving Tegue’s patrol, the May detention of Jairo René Navarrete, a July operation at Morichal and September events at Playitas. He presents Playitas as genuine combat, explicitly distinguishing it from the irregular killings. He repeatedly separates what he saw from information learned afterward.

He invokes fear, military obedience and later attempts to disclose the truth. Questioners challenge why he did not report matters sooner and ask about recruiters, rewards and superior officers. He denies direct knowledge of several alleged payment or statistical systems and says Soto never personally held the result-demand meeting put to him.

Gutiérrez expresses remorse and offers social and educational work as reparation. english_title: Marco Fabián García Céspedes, 26 July 2019: command pressure, staged combat and the Torres family killings
purpose: This substantive session examines García Céspedes’s military trajectory and his participation in deaths presented as combat results. The magistrate asks how intelligence lists, orders, weapons and reporting connected individual incidents to Brigade XVI command structures, while victims’ counsel tests his account.
named_people_roles: García Céspedes describes service with Batallón Rifles, command of a BCG 65 company and later a Brigade XVI special group. Óscar Parra Vera conducts the questioning. He identifies Colonel Henry William Torres Escalante as brigade commander and Major Carlos Alirio Buitrago Bedoya as a superior communicating operational expectations. Soldiers Alzate and Arteaga feature in his incident accounts. Named victims include Cayetano, Fermín Ochoa, Daniel Torres and Roque Julio Torres. Fernando Rodríguez Quecan participates for victims. The roles attributed to other officers are García’s account, not findings adopted by the hearing.

In the Cayetano episode, he says he reported a detention, received a response rejecting capture in favor of a death, and then saw Alzate shoot the man and simulate combat. He qualifies his knowledge of whether the victim slipped or attempted escape. He alleges that later special-group operations answered directly to Torres and that prior involvement was used to pressure him into further results. In the Fermín Ochoa account, he describes placing a supplied weapon beside the body, collective simulated gunfire and moving the body for inspection elsewhere. For the Torres family, he acknowledges personally shooting Daniel Torres and attributes Roque Julio’s shooting to Arteaga. In this session he places Arteaga’s shots first, followed by his own reaction; the September continuation gives a different sequence. The magistrate also explores an earlier Rifles incident and the El Triunfo operation. These accounts distinguish direct conduct from his broader allegations about command knowledge and institutional pressure.
stated_positions_responses: He repeatedly accepts that his conduct was wrong, asks forgiveness and describes the harm as irreparable. His emphasis on pressure and orders accompanies an admission of personal participation rather than a complete denial. He offers symbolic reparation while saying he lacks financial means. Victims’ questioning and judicial follow-up seek concrete corroboration, participants and communications rather than accepting the narrative without examination.
outcome_open_questions: The session is suspended at 19:14 for continuation. Documents are incorporated, further oral and potentially written questions remain, and the magistrate reiterates the need to report security concerns. The exact sequence of the Torres shootings, responsibility for supplied weapons, and links between particular orders and deaths remain matters for comparison with other evidence.

At San Luis de Ariporo, after Modesto Velandia was killed, he describes detaining Yolanda Botía and an unidentified man; he admits firing at the man after an order to kill, and says weapons arrived by helicopter for placement with the bodies. At El Triunfo he helped bring an intoxicated, unarmed Fredy Alexander Sanabria to Casallas and later heard shots. At La Zulia he acknowledges shooting when a man moved toward his waist and says Luz Elena Araque was unarmed. english_title: José Nicolás Siabato Bohórquez: five direct shooting admissions and additional Delta 4 accounts — 18 September 2019
purpose: To obtain Siabato’s account of killings in which he says he directly participated, distinguish those from other operations he witnessed, and clarify orders, false reporting and incentives. The court also examines the personal choices behind his actions and the requirements of restoration.
named_people_roles: Siabato is a professional soldier and combat medic in Delta 4, associated with Counterguerrilla Battalion 23. Óscar Parra Vera presides; Mabel Faride Tejeiro Roa represents him, and Fabiola Lucero Diago Montilla participates for the Public Ministry. Lieutenants Casallas and Nicolás Rodríguez, Sergeant Mateus, Captain Juan Pablo Villota, Lieutenant Edwin Toro and Sergeant Faiber Amaya appear in particular accounts. Fellow soldiers Castellanos, Cigua and Núñez are identified in several operations. Brigade and DAS personnel are discussed, with some higher-level instructions expressly inferred rather than witnessed.
main_accounts_claims: Siabato admits shooting Fredy Alexander Sanabria after his capture in August 2006, describing Casallas’s instruction and a later coordinated combat story. He admits shooting José Serafín Corredor in September after supplying information about his whereabouts; he describes simulated firing and a weapon placed with the body. At Casa Roja in January 2007, he says two detainees were transported separately and that he shot Wilmer Jaimes after hearing the other shooting. For Altos de Purare in January 2008, he admits killing Domingo Pascual Ochoa and placing a recovered rifle; he acknowledges that his account of Villota authorizing the killing is an inference, not a conversation he witnessed. purpose: To answer the JEP questionnaire issued under Auto 125 of July 2019, explaining Ramírez’s work as a GAULA driver, his presence in six questioned operations and the difference he draws between transport, silence and direct killing.
named_people_roles: Ramírez, a former professional soldier and driver, is questioned on the recording by defence lawyer Mabel Faride Tejeiro Roa. He identifies Major Gustavo Soto Bracamonte as GAULA commander and Lieutenant Toro, Captain Rivera, Sergeant Montaña, Sergeant Amaya and Corporal Pérez in particular deployments or orders. Drivers Camargo Pérez and Jhony Higuera figure in transport accounts. Corporal Sajona, soldiers Blanco Avellaneda, Cardona, Campos and Viazus appear in his descriptions of accompanying personnel. He attributes different actions to them with varying certainty and sometimes cannot recall a participant’s full name.
main_accounts_claims: Ramírez describes six operations through his duties transporting soldiers and detained men. At Brisas del Llano in October 2006, he says two men were collected in Villavicencio, transferred between vehicles, taken off-road and killed while he and another driver provided security; the deaths were then reported as combat. He disputes presence at the killing associated with Jorge Acosta in February 2007, saying he exchanged passengers and returned, while an incomplete vehicle log made it appear he remained. At Río Chiquito he describes another Villavicencio pickup, transport and later shots, without claiming to see who fired. At Guayacanal, an extortion-related capture was followed by the man’s killing after investigators had left. For Cuernavaca, he describes two men encountered on the return journey, their detention and appearance of weapons before their deaths. At La Porfía, he recounts police briefly speaking to Rivera, the captives being driven away and killed, and his refusal to sign an ammunition-use record. He says other proceedings involved coached declarations and ammunition records despite his not firing. He admits concealment through failure to report but denies planning operations or killing anyone.
stated_positions_responses: He insists transport instructions appeared lawful and that no one ordered him personally to kill. He invokes threats, possible transfer and command pressure to explain silence, while acknowledging errors and apologizing to families. He disputes treating his role as equivalent to the shooters’ actions and criticizes commanders’ unfulfilled assurances that they would assume responsibility.
outcome_open_questions: Counsel will attach requests for information and responses from military-justice offices to identify further proceedings Ramírez may not recall. He offers to clarify his account and comply with future restorative directions, although he proposes no specific activity. The recording contains no judicial questioning, corroboration or ruling on the disputed transport and shooting roles.

english_title: Jhony Higuera Moreno: driving, concealment and disputed personal shooting roles in GAULA cases — 15 October 2019
purpose: To answer the factual-participation portion of a JEP questionnaire through a recording made with defence counsel. Higuera addresses ten case references, distinguishing transport and concealment he acknowledges from planning, shooting and incidents he says he cannot recall.
named_people_roles: Higuera is a GAULA driver and professional soldier. Denis Rivera Piñeros conducts the recording as defence counsel; no magistrate questions him in this extract. Lieutenants Suancha, Toro, Puentes and Solano, Sergeant Amaya, Corporal Pérez and soldiers Bello, González Almario and others appear in his accounts. He identifies Major Soto and brigade intelligence officer Sarmiento as possible recipients of officers’ calls but expressly says he does not know whom they actually called. Named victims include Eduardo Pérez Vega, Jairo René Navarrete and Arnulfo Tumay Pan.
main_accounts_claims: Higuera describes driving Eduardo Pérez Vega from Villavicencio into Casanare and identifies Bello as the shooter, while denying participation in a killing plan. For Navarrete and Tumay, he describes transport, hearing shots and subsequent body handling, distinguishing observation from others’ identification of shooters. He similarly describes transporting Jonathan Mauricio Parrado and González Delgado, and the pair José Germán Maldonado Achagua and Wilmar Alfonso López Riveros, to places where they were killed; he cannot reliably identify who fired. In Chavinave, he says his objection led to two detainees being removed alive, while a third was taken onward and killed. He retracts his earlier claim that he fired a revolver there, acknowledging a false ammunition form. In La Graciela, his admission goes beyond driving: he says Solano directed him to place and discharge a weapon in a dead man’s hand, and that he complied. He reports only transport or body-recovery roles in La Motus and La Vega, describes La Motus as legitimate combat according to his understanding, and says he has no recollection of the Nunchía case involving Eduard Leandro Estrada Bustos.
stated_positions_responses: Higuera repeatedly denies planning killings or personally shooting victims, but acknowledges complicity through transport, concealment and silence. He attributes his silence to fear and also to preserving opportunities to participate in coleo sport. He reports memory difficulties, offers supporting medical documents if requested, expresses remorse and is willing to seek forgiveness from families.
outcome_open_questions: The recording ends at 10:38 with Higuera available for further requests. Counsel states that questionnaire questions 1–22 will be answered in writing; this recording addresses question 23. There is no judicial ruling or adversarial examination here, and numerous participant identities and details remain uncertain in his recollection.

english_title: Jairo Sánchez Ospina, 15 October 2019: admissions concerning killings and their concealment in GAULA Casanare
purpose: This lawyer-led recording answers only question 14 of the JEP questionnaire: incidents Sánchez knew about or participated in, participants’ roles, killings and the origin of staged weapons. Counsel states that written answers to the remaining questions will accompany the video.
named_people_roles: Jairo Sánchez Ospina describes himself as a GAULA Casanare soldier and driver. Óscar Fernando Salamanca Bernal conducts the recording as his lawyer. Sánchez attributes operational orders to Major Soto, Lieutenant Solano, Corporal Pérez and a senior sergeant named Montaña/Montaño in the transcript. He alleges involvement by soldiers Campos, Blanco, González Almario, Cardona and others, and by a man he identifies as a DAS member using Camilo/El Paisa. His broader allegations also name Brigade XVI commander Torres Escalante.
main_accounts_claims: Sánchez distinguishes early incidents in which he says he only drove or arrived after a death from cases in which he admits shooting. For the March 2007 killing of the person transcribed as Augusto Concha Nieves, he describes collecting a man in Villanueva, transporting him under Solano’s direction and a failed attempt to kill him. He says Solano then ordered him to fire and admits that his shot killed the man. For Alto Cupiagua, he describes detentions, orders to kill, his own gunfire, later delivery of weapons and rearrangement of personnel and ammunition records before statements to investigators. His account includes an unnamed minor and allegations against an intermediary, whose actions are not independently established. For the August 2007 Matepalma deaths of Abelardo Reyes and Abel Antonio Camacho, he describes two separate handovers, transport and renewed orders after an attempted change of plan; he claims responsibility for both deaths. He says false declarations and manipulated accounts concealed what occurred, and characterizes the operation of rewards as profitable for commanders, while saying he received leave rather than money.
stated_positions_responses: He admits personal responsibility and requests forgiveness, while repeatedly presenting obedience, pressure and manipulation by commanders as the explanation for his conduct. He also calls himself a victim of the conflict. He disputes any suggestion that soldiers independently devised the killings, but describes moments when soldiers resisted particular orders or abandoned proposed operations.
outcome_open_questions: The recording closes with counsel’s undertaking to submit it with written questionnaire answers and counsel’s statement that he learned these accounts during this recording. It contains no judicial decision. Command-level knowledge, financial benefits, third-party roles and Sánchez’s descriptions of earlier acquittals or convictions require independent verification.

english_title: Rafael Alejandro Núñez Mejía, 17 October 2019: Delta 4 shooting admission and limits of knowledge about other operations
purpose: The hearing examines Núñez’s service as a combat medic and member of the Delta 4 reaction group, pressures for operational results, and several deaths associated with that unit. The magistrate separates direct participation from false testimony or knowledge gained after other operations.
named_people_roles: Rafael Alejandro Núñez Mejía describes professional-soldier service in BCG 23 and selection for Delta 4 as a combat medic. Juan Carlos Lozada Perdomo presides; Karen Lucía Álvarez Ricardo defends him, Miguel Leonardo Pérez Barrios represents the Procuraduría and María Andrea Ortiz provides psychosocial support. Lieutenant Zamir Humberto Casallas is identified as a Delta 4 commander; Captain Juan Pablo Bellota appears in later episodes. Named victims in other accounts include Freddy Alexander Sanabria, Domingo Pascual Ochoa and Eimer Isidro Mendoza. Núñez cannot name the particular Las Tapias victim he admits shooting.
main_accounts_claims: Núñez alleges repeated radio pressure for combat deaths and says officers sometimes instructed soldiers how to testify, including describing him as a radio operator in an operation he had not attended. For Las Tapias, he recounts three men being seized at a shop after identification by an informant, transported to Hato Corozal and killed. He admits personally shooting one after the lieutenant said they had to be killed, and recalls the victim pleading and warning him of the consequences. He describes clothing or equipment being placed on the men but is uncertain who handled each item. In the Freddy Alexander Sanabria account, he describes pursuit from a gathering and admits firing to simulate combat, while saying he did not see the exact capture or fatal shots. For Domingo Pascual Ochoa, he describes another group taking a person uphill and hearing shots, without witnessing the death. For Eimer Isidro Mendoza, he attributes the shooting to Castellanos and says a revolver was then placed on the unarmed man. The magistrate challenges chronology inconsistent with his account of leaving Delta 4 for nursing studies.
stated_positions_responses: He expresses remorse, asks forgiveness and recognizes the harm of taking life, while emphasizing pressure from commanders and the consequences for lower-ranking soldiers. He repeatedly distinguishes direct knowledge from assumptions, forgotten dates and cases linked to him through earlier statements. His closing remarks combine willingness to repair with continuing frustration about military leadership and the constraints he believes security forces face.
outcome_open_questions: The hearing closes at 18:19. The magistrate asks him to provide written detail if his memory improves. He offers to undertake restorative work but presents no concrete project. Outstanding matters include the chronology of his assignments, the identity of his Las Tapias victim, responsibility in indirectly observed episodes and the content of earlier false statements.

english_title: César Augusto Cómbita Eslava — third session on recruiting networks, Roger Acero and further disputed incidents, 18 October 2019
purpose: The third 2019 session examines how special groups shared personnel, victims and resources, then tests Cómbita’s role in additional deaths. It distinguishes direct acts, intelligence-paperwork involvement, knowledge supplied by fellow soldiers and events in which he denies participation.
named_people_roles: Cómbita answers Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera with Ángela Patricia Bernal Guzmán as counsel. He identifies Burgos Jiménez, Gustavo Parada and Gabriel Bonilla as participants in obtaining or moving victims; Puerto Marcolino and Carlos Manuel Angarita Reyes appear in his allegations about staff support and concealment. Soldier García Comayán is the source of a recollection concerning Roger Acero. Other victims discussed include José Arcadio Rodríguez, Jesid Fonseca Pesca, Diego Armando Heredia Monroy, Domingo Antonio Zorro Castro, Luis Alberto Pinto and Saúl Céspedes.
main_accounts_claims: Cómbita says recruiting could cross company boundaries and describes Parada’s work locating people for different groups. He alleges participation by some DAS personnel and explains that falsified reward records could justify spending on fuel, weapons and other operational needs. His most significant additional admission concerns Roger Acero and José Arcadio Rodríguez at La Graciela: after conversations with soldiers, he accepts that he took García Comayán’s rifle and killed the wounded Acero. He explicitly grounds that account partly in the soldier’s recollection and cannot describe Rodríguez’s death with equivalent detail. He denies direct participation in several other cases, including the deaths of Fonseca and Heredia/Zorro, while accepting responsibility for knowing about unlawful practices or for documents bearing his signature. Regarding Pinto, he describes a possible transport role rather than recruitment or presence at the shooting. For the September episode involving Saúl Céspedes, he relays Parada’s account of attracting men with a proposed armed-group recruitment exercise and acknowledges receiving information while the victims were alive. The magistrate presses why he did not intervene.
stated_positions_responses: Cómbita accepts failure to prevent, report or oppose conduct he knew about, while contesting accusations that make him the organizer of every death. He attributes his silence partly to fear of losing his career. He maintains that commanders and operations staff also enabled the system, but the summary preserves those statements as allegations, not resolved allocations of responsibility.
outcome_open_questions: Further comparison, victims’ observations and questioning are left open because the three-session review does not exhaust the incident list. The source leaves important uncertainty about memories reconstructed with fellow detainees, individual shooting roles, dates and the distinction between signing supporting documents and directing a specific killing.

english_title: Giovanni Montaño Arboleda: admissions and disputed accounts from the BIRNO special group
purpose: The 21 October 2019 hearing examines Montaño’s service in the Ramón Nonato Pérez Battalion’s special group and his knowledge of killings presented as combat deaths. Questions separate his own shootings, security duties, observations and assumptions about superior orders.
named_people_roles: Montaño is a professional soldier who served in BIRNO 44 before joining the Casanare military GAULA. Óscar Parra Vera conducts the questioning; Denis Bibiana Rivera Piñeros is defense counsel and Pedro Clímaco García Barragán represents the Public Ministry. Montaño identifies successive special-group commanders Miguel Andrés Sierra García, Gildardo Jiménez Castrillón and Oliver Cárdenas Gil. Fauner José Barahona appears in his account as a civilian who brought people to the troops. These descriptions convey testimony, not findings against the named people.
main_accounts_claims: Montaño describes a detained motorcyclist killed near Río Chiquito and says Hugo Edgar Araque was detained and then killed after Sierra ordered subordinates to do so; he did not see Araque’s actual shooting. He calls the deaths of Armando Collazos and Javier Garcés unlawful and describes other soldiers firing while the remaining group provided security and simulated combat. He admits shooting Edilson Mendoza Soto with Jiménez and Dumar Rodríguez, says Mendoza had a weapon but had not fired, and retracts an earlier account that concealed the shooters. He also retracts the claim that Gustavo Adolfo Wilkin Correa was shot for ignoring a checkpoint. Regarding René Ojeda, he admits firing the final shot after Ojeda had already been wounded, and attributes the victims’ arrival to Barahona. He describes shooting an unidentified, unarmed man who ran from troops under Cárdenas, while denying that Cárdenas expressly ordered that shooting. Finally, he admits killing one of two unarmed men, Luis Uriel Casiano Murillo and Joel Bernal Barrera, after Jiménez assigned one to him and the other to Tarache. In contrast, he maintains that the August 2005 Pajarito deaths resulted from actual combat.
stated_positions_responses: Montaño regrets obeying unlawful instructions and failing to report earlier events. He cites limited schooling, pressure on soldiers and fear of reprisals when explaining his conduct, while acknowledging his own participation. He distinguishes matters he witnessed from uncertain dates, unknown planning and inferred intelligence involvement. He proposes craft training and talks to soldiers and families as possible reparative contributions.
outcome_open_questions: Parra requests a personal written or recorded supplement by 21 November, especially on other incidents, direct perpetrators, orders and concealment. The closing describes eleven events discussed and anticipates victims’ responses and further comparison with evidence. Identifying the unnamed victim and clarifying planning beyond Montaño’s direct observations remain open.

english_title: Pedro José Roa Alvarado, 21 October 2019: five BIRNO incidents and suspension over a potential defense conflict
purpose: Roa’s initial oral version examines his movement from BIRNO combat units to a special group and intelligence, then develops five killing accounts. New allegations concerning another officer represented by the same lawyer lead to a procedural question about possible conflicting defense interests.
named_people_roles: Roa speaks as a former BIRNO 44 soldier. Óscar Parra Vera presides, Javier Humberto Núñez Jiménez is defense counsel, and Pedro Clímaco García Barragán represents the Procuraduría. Roa identifies Lieutenant Miguel Andrés Sierra García, Sergeant Gildardo Jiménez and intelligence personnel César Augusto Cómbita Eslava, Gustavo Parada Cuéllar, Guzmán Pistala and Wilfrido Domínguez. Lieutenant Johan Leonardo Rivera Muñoz is central to the potential conflict. The Los Mangos victims are named as Jhon Fabio Daza Domínguez, José Ernel Garzón Sánchez and Einer Henry Melo Gutiérrez.
main_accounts_claims: Roa says he entered the special group in April 2006 and later requested transfer after seeing operations outside lawful limits, only to encounter further concealment in intelligence. At Puente Tabla, he admits shooting on Sierra’s order and says the purpose was to implicate him so he could not report others. He infers that the two victims expected work, while acknowledging he does not know exactly how they were recruited. He describes a security role in the San Benito/Cusiana episode, a motorcyclist’s seizure and transport toward Banco del Oso, and the killing of William Salamanca Cruz near Tauramena’s former rubbish site. In those accounts, he distinguishes hearing gunfire and seeing the aftermath from observing the actual shooter. For Los Mangos in July 2007, he alleges that Cómbita detained three men in Aguazul, arranged their placement and killed one himself while directing Rivera to take responsibility for the other two. Roa says he directly saw Cómbita’s shooting but cannot identify which person fired the other shots. He describes subsequent coordination of the report and soldiers’ judicial accounts.

Defense counsel says the Los Mangos attribution is new to him and may conflict with his representation of Rivera in ordinary and JEP proceedings. The Procuraduría supports pausing to protect procedural rights; the magistrate does not decide the factual conflict.
outcome_open_questions: At 16:27 the hearing is suspended. Counsel receives three weeks, until November 11, to explain the potential conflict and any necessary change of representation. Continuation may be oral or written after that issue is assessed. The court asks Roa to consider harm and restoration, but no detailed reparative proposal is heard.

english_title: Jairo Alonso Perdomo Rincón — voluntary statement, 22 October 2019
purpose: To explain Perdomo’s administrative work in BIRNO’s operations section, examine how orders and results were documented, and establish what he knew about four questioned incidents while allowing further access to files needed for his defence.
named_people_roles: Sergeant Jairo Alonso Perdomo Rincón appears with lawyer Luz Marina Achury before Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera; Germán Rincón Cuellar questions him for the Public Ministry. He identifies Colonel Hernán Acosta Pardo as battalion commander and discusses Lieutenant César Augusto Cómbita Eslava in relation to intelligence and operational documents. The questioner identifies incidents involving Olimpo Tinjacá, Andrés Alfonso Sanabria, Carlos José Esquivel and Pablo César Murillo, and John Fabio Daza, José Ernel Garzón and Geinar Melo. Perdomo denies knowing those victims personally.

He says commanders could issue verbal or radio instructions before written documents were completed. His central defence is that authenticating a document meant certifying its preparation in the operations section, not authorizing a mission or ordering a killing. He says his rank did not empower him to direct the officers or patrols concerned. He accepts delivering operational orders but denies intelligence collection, handling weapons for victims, visiting killing sites or participating in body recovery. english_title: Manuel Guillermo Torres Ramírez, 25 October 2019: admissions concerning José Albeiro Joya and a family killed near the Pisba River
purpose: Torres Ramírez is questioned about two incidents, how the killings were reported as combat, and the officers and soldiers involved. The hearing also examines military training, his relationship with a superior who provided financial assistance, and his proposed contribution to truth and reparation.
named_people_roles: Torres Ramírez describes commanding Diluvio 5 in BCG 29 and the battalion’s Escorpión special group, explicitly distinguishing it from the brigade’s special group. He names Major Jairo Gabriel Paguay Escobar as battalion commander. Soldier Holman Cuevas Arenas and soldier Pineda appear in the José Albeiro Joya Rodríguez account; Jefferson/Yeferson Rincón Ortiz appears in the Pisba account. The transcript identifies the presiding magistrate by initials HEGD. The second incident concerns members of the Maldonado and Tabaco Socha families, including a woman whose pregnancy he says he learned about later.

He admits insisting that Cuevas carry out the order, identifying the victim to him, retrieving a pistol after the shooting, and directing a false combat presentation. He describes Pineda placing the weapon in the victim’s hand and soldiers firing to simulate an engagement. For the December 2005 Pisba River incident, he says soldiers fired toward a shelter and killed two men; a wounded woman told him they were civilians who had been fishing and hiding from gunfire. He denies receiving a specific incentive for these two incidents and treats the later financial help as assistance, a characterization the magistrate challenges.

english_title: Helbert Pérez García — continued voluntary statement, 6 December 2019
purpose: To continue Pérez’s March testimony about unlawful deaths attributed to the Casanare GAULA and BIRNO, clarify his participation and command relationships, and obtain responses to accounts by other soldiers and questions raised for victims.
named_people_roles: Pérez appears as a former noncommissioned officer, with Jimmy Fernando Niño Torres defending him. Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera presides; Germán Rincón Cuellar represents the Public Ministry and Luis Fernando Rodríguez Quecán questions him for victims. Óscar Parra Vera and auxiliary magistrate Juan Pablo Cardona direct the questioning; Rocío del Pilar Bonilla represents Pereira. His accounts attribute directions to Major Soto, Lieutenant Suancha, Sergeant Gustavo Montaña and Corporal Pérez. He identifies soldiers and intelligence-linked intermediaries in particular episodes, while disclaiming access to reserved funds and higher-level administrative decisions.

He recounts the June 2007 killing of an unidentified woman: he says information attributed to intelligence-linked contacts led to her being taken from Yopal, intercepted by GAULA, dressed in military-style clothing and killed. He denies firing in that incident and says she was buried unidentified in Paz de Ariporo. In his Macedonia 25 account, an intended operation near Villavicencio failed; on the return journey, two people encountered on the road were detained. He alleges that Soto authorized killing them despite their lack of weapons and that Montaña and a soldier shot them near Cuernavaca. english_title: Jorge Antonio Solano Galvis: GAULA planning, concealed participation and the killing of a wounded woman — 27 July 2020

Major Gustavo Soto is the commander whom Solano identifies as organizing operations through trusted personnel. Corporal Pérez, soldier González Almario and Lieutenant Suancha appear in particular operational accounts. Colonel William Torres Escalante is discussed as brigade commander, with Solano distinguishing some observations from assumptions about his knowledge. Fabiola Castro is the woman named in the court’s questions about the May 2007 operation.
main_accounts_claims: Solano describes a pattern in which Soto and trusted personnel planned an operation, then assigned another officer to accompany it and later provide the official account. He says participants could be omitted from patrol reports while others appeared in ammunition records despite not firing. He admits concealing killings and failing to report them, while disputing that nominal command proves he planned every operation. For Mate Palma on 27 June 2007, he attributes planning and direction to Suancha and says Soto assigned him the subsequent declarations to conceal Suancha’s involvement. He acknowledges presence and cover-up. Regarding Alto Cupiagua on 8 May 2007, Solano says he planned an ambush against people reportedly extorting a farmer. He describes Fabiola Castro surviving the initial gunfire, being transported while gravely wounded, and receiving another shot from someone he cannot identify with certainty. He initially presents the operation as combat but acknowledges that the final shot was omitted from the account given to investigators. Questions probe medical assistance, weapons and the basis for identifying her as a guerrilla member. He also corrects a confusion between La Graciela and Buenavista case files.

He nevertheless insists that responsibility must distinguish planning, shooting, presence and false reporting. His claim that Torres must have known partly rests on military hierarchy and the volume of reported results; he does not present every inference as a witnessed order.
outcome_open_questions: The court treats the oral and written accounts as material requiring comparison with other evidence. It arranges access to the recording and written statement, fixes 6 August for additional questions, and provides for a subsequent written response. english_title: Gustavo Vargas Vargas — voluntary statement, 23 September 2020
purpose: To clarify Vargas’s command of Counterguerrilla Battalion 23, his relationship to the Delta 4 platoon and his response to accounts implicating him in the April 2007 operation in which three people were killed and reported as combat deaths.

english_title: Carlos Manuel Angarita Reyes — operations responsibilities, disputed signatures and seven alleged unlawful-killing incidents
purpose: This session examines Angarita’s responsibilities at the Ramón Nonato Pérez Battalion, his authentication of operational records, and his knowledge of seven alleged killings presented as combat deaths. Questions test his distinction between holding an operations post and exercising effective command.
named_people_roles: Carlos Manuel Angarita Reyes is the principal interviewee and a former battalion operations officer who also describes acting in executive and command posts. Nancy Acosta assists his defense. Angarita identifies Germán Alberto León Durán and Acosta as battalion commanders, William Torres Escalante as brigade commander, and Marcolino Puerto as the officer who, he says, performed operations functions during his absence. Victims’ representatives and the Public Ministry question his documentary account and seek access to supporting records.
main_accounts_claims: Angarita says he complained to León Durán that he could not exercise his assigned operations role, but was told to obey the command arrangement. He says Puerto and other staff performed those functions while he served away from headquarters. He nevertheless accepts authenticating tactical missions and ammunition records, including potentially after operations, explaining that written records could formalize earlier verbal orders and that he trusted the intelligence, signatures and lawful instructions they contained. He recalls operational pressure, an occasion involving a demand for two combat deaths, and comparative results tables, while qualifying how often he heard numerical demands. He explicitly says he knew what the supposed missions involved and describes carrying weapons and other items to place with victims. He says he challenged a rumor of payment to kill a particular person, while accepting Soto’s distinction between that and killing alleged offenders. For Epopeya on 12 June 2006, he identifies Edwin Alexander Camargo Alarcón as the victim and says he witnessed Sánchez shoot him while handcuffed. english_title: Wilson Camargo Tamayo, 21 January 2021: acknowledgment of concealment in Operation Destello and defense of other GAULA operations

He describes Murillo’s shooting of an unarmed civilian as an operational error based on mistaken threat perception. english_title: Guillermo Quiñónez Quiroz — voluntary statement, 12 February 2021

english_title: Cipriano Peña Chivatá — brigade command, operational pressure and responses to warning signs
purpose: The first session examines Peña’s assumption of command of Brigade 16 in July 2007, command and intelligence arrangements, demands for operational results, and responses to suspected unlawful killings. It also addresses aspects of his preceding command of Mobile Brigade 12.
named_people_roles: Retired Colonel Cipriano Peña Chivatá gives the account. Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera presides; Jairo Andrés Santos Peñaloza represents Peña, and Carmen Giovanna Restrepo Medina intervenes for the Public Ministry. William Torres Escalante is his predecessor at Brigade 16; Generals Quiñones and Mario Montoya feature in questions about superior-command demands. Accounts attributed to Wilson de Jesús Soto Bracamonte, John Alexander Suancha Florián and Jaime Alberto Rivera Mahecha are put to Peña for response. main_accounts_claims: Peña describes taking over an established operational plan and relying on staff, unit commanders and judicial authorities. He says he returned the special Delta groups to their battalions’ control because a brigade should direct rather than execute operations. He portrays superior demands as enforcing lawful security responsibilities, rejects treating demands for results as authorization to kill civilians, and does not affirm quoted expressions attributed to Montoya as his own recollection. Confronted with Soto’s account that unlawful practices continued under his command, Peña disputes an inference that he knew or authorized them. He says he made GAULA personnel available when prosecutors requested their arrest and distinguishes their legal representation from an appointment by the brigade. He also recounts warning staff against illegality, meeting civilian authorities and hearing community complaints, including assisting a complainant’s family. For Mobile Brigade 12, he points to periods of leave and says he arranged an investigative reconstruction when allegations arose. Throughout, he argues that effective oversight operated through staff, communications and judicial processes rather than the commander’s presence at every operation.

Parra and victims’ counsel press for concrete answers about warning signs, unidentified bodies, numerical targets and what followed complaints. The Public Ministry also challenges broad contextual answers that leave specific questions unresolved. Peña contests attributing other officers’ conduct to him merely because he held command.

english_title: Carlos Alirio Buitrago Bedoya — BCG 65, Delta 6 and disputed command knowledge, 26 February 2021

Statements by Marco Fabián García Céspedes are put to him alongside questions about signatures, operational reports and oversight.
named_people_roles: Carlos Alirio Buitrago Bedoya is the former BCG 65 commander. Martín Antonio Moreno Sanjuán presides; José Yair Toro Buitrago is defense counsel; Fernando Rodríguez Kekhan and Julieth Nayibe Moreno Vargas represent victims. Lieutenant Marco Fabián García Céspedes commanded troops implicated in the incidents and later Delta 6. Henry William Torres Escalante commanded Brigade 16. The cases concern José Cayetano Mendivelso, Fermín Ochoa Barrios, Roque Julio Torres and his minor son, and Alcides Castillo Fonseca.
main_accounts_claims: Buitrago separates the killing of José Cayetano Mendivelso, when García’s unit was directly under him, from later Delta 6 operations. He says he ordered a genuine intelligence-led infiltration, received a fabricated combat report and tried to send Sergeant Palomino’s support, which García stopped. He denies the allegation that he ordered Mendivelso’s execution and denies supplying a list of people to kill. For Fermín Ochoa’s death, he admits eventually authorizing Delta 6 to enter his area after insisting it not disrupt another operation; he says he learned only later that a murder occurred. For the Torres father and son, he denies prior operational knowledge and says subsequent case files supplied the details. For Alcides Castillo, he recalls Delta 6 being sent to reinforce troops after an actual attack but says he did not know the subsequent unlawful conduct. More generally, he acknowledges signing Delta operational orders and receiving its statistics while asserting that the brigade controlled deployment and permissions. He describes his signatures as administrative and says the documents appeared lawful, without conferring with García before signing.
stated_positions_responses: Buitrago accepts that the deaths were grave unlawful acts but rejects García’s claims about his knowledge and orders. english_title: Juan Pablo Bravo, 9 April 2021: alleged simulated combat and coercion to sign false operational accounts
purpose: Bravo answers a JEP questionnaire in a lawyer-led recorded submission addressed to Magistrate Óscar Parra Vera. He explains four criminal proceedings, his military service and claimed role in disputed operations, then responds to questions about responsibility, incentives, victims and non-repetition.
named_people_roles: Juan Pablo Bravo describes himself as a former professional soldier associated with a special group operating under Brigade XVI. Mabel Faride Tejeiro, his defence lawyer, reads the questionnaire and structures the recording; the magistrate is its addressee rather than an audible examiner. Bravo identifies Lieutenant Juan Pablo Gutiérrez and Lieutenant Marco Fabián García Céspedes as commanders involved in his accounts. He also mentions soldiers Arteaga, Socha, Cano and Gaitán Zambrano, and contrasts the conduct of a senior noncommissioned officer identified as Úsuga with that of the lieutenants.
main_accounts_claims: Bravo recounts operations in the Campo Hermoso area, El Tablón, El Triunfo and Los Lirios. He says gunfire presented as combat was sometimes generated by the troops themselves, and that soldiers were subsequently inserted into ammunition-expenditure reports and instructed to repeat a false combat narrative. For one proceeding he claims he did not attend the operation but nevertheless signed such documentation. In the El Triunfo sequence, he describes a roadside stop of a woman identified to troops as a nurse, her transfer to another military vehicle, and a later search said to concern wounded guerrillas. He says the people at the rural location appeared to him to be civilians and alleges that the reported combat account was fabricated. In the Los Lirios account, associated in his opening with Alcides Castillo’s death, he places himself on security duties and says he heard orders to fire without seeing the killing. He denies firing his rifle in these events, while acknowledging that he initially repeated false accounts. He contrasts these episodes with patrols under Úsuga where pressure for results allegedly did not produce fabricated deaths.

english_title: Guillermo Quiñónez Quiroz — continued voluntary statement, 10 June 2021
purpose: To test the retired general’s account of Fourth Division command responsibilities, operational oversight and responses to warnings about unlawful deaths, using documents, Public Ministry questions and victims’ challenges following his February statement.
named_people_roles: Retired Major General Guillermo Quiñónez Quiroz appears with defence lawyer Pedro Jairo Condia Torres. Óscar Parra Vera presides, accompanied by auxiliary magistrates Paula Andrea Acosta and Martín Antonio Moreno San Juan. Carmen Giovanna Restrepo Medina represents the Public Ministry. Victims’ lawyers include José Ramiro Orjuela Aguilar and María Paula Lemus. Colonel Torres is discussed as a brigade commander with tactical planning responsibilities, and Major Soto Bracamonte as the detained GAULA commander whose case raised questions about Quiñónez’s knowledge and response.
main_accounts_claims: Quiñónez maintains that division command set broad objectives while brigades and tactical units planned and conducted their operations. He describes legitimacy, territorial control and weakening armed groups’ capacity as his objectives, rather than an instruction to produce unlawful deaths. Confronted with documents referring to numerous questioned cases and investigative inspections, he recalls prosecutorial visits, slow investigations and inadequate investigative resources. He says the division shifted effort toward assisting prosecutors and military judges as fighting diminished. He explains command authority through doctrine and disciplinary rules and argues that corrective measures required sufficient information. As preventive mechanisms, he describes an open-door policy, anonymous written reports from personnel and direct channels for civilians’ complaints. Victims’ representatives challenge whether he personally confronted commanders or prevented further killings after warnings. He says reports received through the chain of command had not appeared illegitimate and expressly denies suspecting fabricated information. He distinguishes assisting investigations from controlling their conclusions and rejects the suggestion that he classified every questioned death as collateral damage. Asked about sympathy for detained Soto compared with victims, he distinguishes what he says he knew then from his present distress after learning more.
stated_positions_responses: He defends the adequacy of his formal command procedures and repeatedly assigns factual determination to competent investigators. Defence counsel objects to questions considered speculative, and the magistrate reiterates the hearing’s dialogical purpose. Victims seek concrete actions and answers about foreseeability, rather than general doctrine; Quiñónez largely responds with institutional procedures, documentary explanations and denials of contemporaneous knowledge.
outcome_open_questions: The session is suspended at 15:02, with another hearing to address Meta more specifically. The record leaves disputed whether warning signs should have prompted stronger preventive action, how effective disciplinary monitoring was, and whether the general’s claimed lack of knowledge is consistent with the documents and other testimony.

This summary reports the general’s procedural and legal claims without adopting them as a legal determination; the February testimony is a separate record.

english_title: Clovis Arbey Duque Vega — sworn testimony on DAS Casanare reports and joint operations, 30 June 2021
purpose: The source template is headed as a voluntary version, but the hearing expressly receives Duque’s sworn testimony. The questions examine DAS Casanare’s organization, information-sharing with Brigade 16, authorization and review of officers’ reports, and his knowledge of specified operations involving deaths presented as combat casualties.
named_people_roles: Clovis Arbey Duque Vega is a former DAS official who held operational coordination and administrative roles and says he later joined the CTI. He appears without counsel. Óscar Parra Vera opens the session and Martín Antonio Moreno Sanjuán conducts questioning; Carmen Jhoana Restrepo Medina and victims’ lawyers Fernando Rodríguez and Julieth Moreno participate. Duque identifies Orlando Rivas as departmental DAS director, Servio Tulio Fula in judicial police, Fernando Bernal Herrera as a report author, and Neider Calderón in an account of a false attendance report.
main_accounts_claims: Duque describes a hierarchy in which the director chose personnel and coordinated with other institutions, intelligence staff processed sources, and judicial police reviewed investigators’ reports. He says his signature often supplied an administrative endorsement after the immediate supervisor’s review. He distinguishes the departmental DAS office from DAS personnel assigned to GAULA, who had a separate chain of command. He acknowledges contributing source information and signing work orders or operational plans but denies planning killings, joining operations that produced deaths or receiving contemporaneous accounts of unlawful acts. When questioned about the Freddy Alexander Sanabria/Centella documentation and a congratulation in his record, he attributes his role to supplying information rather than participating in the shooting. The magistrate presses the difference between signing an operational plan and endorsing a completed report. In the Las Tapias case for which he says proceedings against him were terminated, Duque adds that Calderón later told him he had not attended the operation despite writing as if he had; Duque says he learned this only after the officer’s detention. He repeatedly identifies limited recollection or refers questions to those present at the scene.
stated_positions_responses: Duque maintains that the orders he saw concerned verification and lawful procedures, with no apparent instruction to kill. He says he would have questioned or reported an irregularity had it been evident, while acknowledging that closer reading could reveal concerns. He emphasizes the region’s security conditions and denies that passing intelligence amounted to selecting someone for execution.
outcome_open_questions: The sworn statement closes at 12:54. The questions leave unresolved how thoroughly endorsing officials reviewed reports, whether source information was verified, and when supervisors learned of falsification. The record distinguishes cases involving departmental DAS personnel from those involving the separately organized GAULA component, requiring case-specific follow-up.
